To fly in the face of something means to openly go against it, defy it, or contradict it — especially when that thing is widely accepted, well-established, or considered obvious.

The "something" is usually:

  • Evidence or facts
  • Logic or reason
  • Common sense
  • Tradition or convention
  • Authority or warnings

So when you say an action or idea "flies in the face of" something, you're saying it boldly goes against what most people accept as true, safe, or sensible.

To understand an idiom well, you need to understand the image it paints in your mind.

Picture an angry bird — a crow, a rooster, or any fierce bird. When threatened or provoked, it doesn't run away. Instead, it flies straight at your face — wings beating, beak pointed directly at you. It is confrontational, aggressive, and defiant. It challenges you head-on.

That is exactly what this idiom captures. When something "flies in the face of" evidence, for example, it is charging directly at that evidence, refusing to back down, and openly contradicting it. The key feeling is bold, direct defiance.
The Tone and Feeling of the Idiom

This is important: the idiom almost always carries a negative or critical tone.

When you say something flies in the face of evidence or reason, you are usually criticising it. You're suggesting it is:

  • Wrong
  • Reckless
  • Stubborn
  • Illogical

The idiom implies that the thing being defied — reason, evidence, tradition — has genuine weight and authority. So defying it isn't brave; it's foolish or irresponsible.

Think of it this way: if a doctor gives you advice backed by decades of medical science and you ignore it, your behaviour flies in the face of medical expertise. The idiom signals that something is going against a force that deserves to be respected — and that's why it sounds so negative.
What You Usually Pair It With

The idiom almost always appears in the pattern:

"fly in the face of + [respected thing]"

Here are the most natural and common pairings:

  • fly in the face of evidence
  • fly in the face of reason / logic
  • fly in the face of common sense
  • fly in the face of the facts
  • fly in the face of convention / tradition
  • fly in the face of authority
  • fly in the face of nature
  • fly in the face of danger (less common; see below)

Here are clear, natural examples to help you see the idiom in action:

1. "His claim that the earth is only a few thousand years old flies in the face of all scientific evidence."
→ His claim boldly contradicts what science has firmly established.

2. "Spending your last savings on lottery tickets flies in the face of common sense."
→ It openly goes against what any sensible person would call logical behaviour.

3. "The new law flies in the face of decades of legal tradition in this country."
→ The law contradicts and defies how things have long been done.

4. "She continued to smoke even after the doctor's warning, flying in the face of medical advice."
→ She openly defied advice that was clearly in her best interest.

5. "The politician's speech flies in the face of the very values his party claims to stand for."
→ His speech directly contradicts and undermines those values.
A Special Case: "Fly in the Face of Danger"

You may occasionally hear "fly in the face of danger." This usage is slightly different. Here, the idiom means to boldly confront danger without fear — it is closer to admiring someone's courage rather than criticising their foolishness. However, this use is much rarer. In the vast majority of cases, the idiom is used critically.

Stick to the critical/negative usage in your own speech and writing. It is far more common and is the core meaning.

The idiom dates back several centuries in the English language and is rooted in the literal behaviour of birds.

In earlier English, the phrase originally meant a bird (or sometimes an insect) that aggressively flies straight at someone's face — an act of raw, confrontational defiance. Fighting birds, like roosters, were known for launching themselves face-first at their opponents. This image of charging directly at something with aggression and boldness was then borrowed into figurative language.

Over time, people began using it metaphorically: if your idea or action "flies in the face of" reason, it is as if your idea is charging straight at reason with aggressive disregard — refusing to be tamed by it.
How It Is Different From Similar Idioms

It helps to compare it with related expressions:

  • "Goes against" — very similar in meaning, but more neutral and everyday. "Fly in the face of" sounds stronger and more dramatic.
  • "Flies in the face of" vs. "turns a blind eye to" — "turning a blind eye" means ignoring something deliberately. "Flying in the face of" means actively contradicting or defying it. One is passive avoidance; the other is active opposition.
  • "Thumbs your nose at" — also means to defy or show disrespect, but is more informal and often more playful. "Fly in the face of" is more formal and serious.
  • "Flies in the face of" vs. "bucks the trend" — "bucking the trend" just means doing something different from the norm, often in an admirable or interesting way. "Flying in the face of" is stronger and more negative — it suggests you're defying something that has genuine authority or truth.

A few quick notes to help you use it correctly:

  • It is always followed by "of" — you cannot say "fly in the face" alone and stop there.
  • The verb changes with the subject: flies, flew, flying, flown — it conjugates like any normal verb.
    • "This decision flies in the face of logic."
    • "The new findings flew in the face of what we believed."
    • "He was flying in the face of all warnings."
  • It is mostly used in written and formal spoken English, though it does appear in everyday conversation too.

"Fly in the face of" means to boldly and openly defy or contradict something well-established — usually evidence, reason, logic, or tradition — and it almost always signals that the defiance is wrong, reckless, or foolish.

Once you hold that image in your mind — of an angry bird flying straight at your face in open challenge — the idiom will never feel abstract again.
